notes.meaning: Abram left Egypt and traveled back up into the dry southern part of Canaan with his wife, his nephew Lot, and everything he owned. God had kept them safe and allowed them to return without harm, even after their mistakes in Egypt. Abram did not let the comforts or wealth of Egypt keep him from returning to the land God had promised.

Abram was very wealthy, owning great herds of livestock as well as silver and gold. His riches were a sign of the Lord's generous blessing on his journey. Even with all these worldly goods, Abram kept his devotion to God and did not let wealth weigh down his spiritual life.

Abram traveled by stages from the southern desert toward Bethel, packing and pitching his tents as he went. He headed straight for the hill between Bethel and Ai where he had camped when he first arrived in Canaan. Visiting familiar ground helped him remember the close fellowship he had once enjoyed with God there.

Abram arrived at the exact spot where he had previously built an altar, and there he prayed to the Lord. Even if the old stone altar was no longer standing, he renewed his worship and gave thanks for God's protection. True faith always expresses itself in regular prayer and thankful worship.

Lot had traveled alongside his uncle and had also become very prosperous, owning his own flocks, herds, and tents. Living in Abram's company had brought Lot a share in God's outward blessings. Having many tents showed that Lot now led a large household of servants and workers.

The pastures could not supply enough grass and water to feed both men's large herds at the same time. Their possessions had grown so great that the two households could no longer live side by side. Possessions that people often hope will bring peace ended up driving two close family members apart.

Arguments soon broke out between Abram's herdsmen and Lot's herdsmen over good grazing spots and wells. The danger was even greater because the Canaanites and Perizzites were already occupying much of the surrounding territory. Quarrels between people who worship God give their unbelieving neighbors an excuse to look down on their faith.

Abram stepped forward right away to stop the argument before it could damage their family bond. He reminded Lot that they were close kinsmen who shared the same faith, making fighting completely unfitting. Even though Abram was the older and respected leader, he spoke gently and made the first move to seek peace.

Abram generously offered Lot first choice of any direction in the countryside so they could separate in peace. Abram held the divine promise to the land and had every right to choose first, but he surrendered his claim for the sake of harmony. He trusted that God would provide for him no matter what region was left over.

Lot surveyed the Jordan valley and saw that the whole region toward Zoar was rich with water and lush grass. Before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, that valley looked as fertile as the garden of Eden or the well-watered plains of Egypt. Lot focused entirely on outward beauty and physical wealth without considering his spiritual wellbeing.

Lot picked the entire green Jordan valley for himself and journeyed eastward to claim it. Instead of showing respect to his older uncle by letting Abram choose, Lot eagerly took the finest territory. The two men parted company quietly, but Lot's greedy decision soon led him into deep trouble.

Abram stayed in the hill country of Canaan, living as a traveler in tents, while Lot settled down among the cities of the valley. Lot gradually moved his campsite until his tents were set up right next to Sodom. Drifting closer to the corrupt city opened the door to spiritual compromise.

The people living in Sodom were openly wicked and committed terrible sins against the Lord without any shame. Their abundant food and easy life only fed their pride and rebellious behavior. Lot had gained rich grazing land, but he had placed himself in great spiritual peril among ungodly neighbors.

After Lot had left, the Lord spoke to Abram to comfort him in his loneliness. God invited him to look out across the countryside in all four directions from the high hill where he stood. What God had prepared for Abram by faith was far greater than what Lot had grabbed for himself by sight.

God promised to give all the land Abram could see to him and his family line forever. Separating from Lot showed that the promised inheritance belonged strictly to Abram's line rather than his nephew's. God made sure that Abram's willing sacrifice for the sake of peace did not cost him anything in the end.

differ.view: The promise of the land forever pointed forward to Christ and finds its final fulfillment in the heavenly country given to all believers.

notes.meaning: God pledged that Abram's future descendants would be so numerous that they could no more be counted than the dust of the ground. This was an astonishing promise, because Abram was already an old man and still had no children. The promise taught Abram to trust God's word rather than what seemed naturally possible.

God instructed Abram to walk through the entire land to explore its length and width. By walking across the territory, he was claiming it by faith as God's gift to his family. It reminded him that he was still a pilgrim for now, looking forward to the day God would hand it over.

Abram moved his campsite south and settled near the large oak trees of Mamre at Hebron. There he built an altar where he could offer animal sacrifices and give thanks to God. Worship remained the central focus of Abram's household wherever he pitched his tent.
